claims.claim: Long-term follow-up of cell dissemination from cell-in-cell structures indicated that each cell maintains its initial single labelling color.
claims.source: Furthermore, long-term follow-up of cell dissemination from this structure indicated that each cell maintains its initial single labelling color (Figure 6—video 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse video microscopy.

claims.claim: Blocking ROCK almost completely prevented T cell-mediated cell-in-cell formation.
claims.source: Given the similarity of this formation to entosis, we used ROCK inhibitor, which is the key regulator of this process. Indeed, blocking ROCK almost completely prevented T cell-mediated cell-in-cell formation (Figure 6B, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: There was no increase or changes in the cellular localization of phosphorylated β catenin, E-cadherin, and phosphorylated integrin β1 in cell-in-cell structures.
claims.source: However, we observed no increase or changes in the cellular localization of phosphorylated β catenin, E-cadherin, and phosphorylated integrin β1 (26) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting other mediators promote this entosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: There was no reduction in cell-in-cell formation upon blocking of E- and N- cadherins, or inhibition of Wnt signaling.
claims.source: Furthermore, there was no reduction in cell-in-cell formation upon blocking of E- and N- cadherins, or inhibition of Wnt signaling (Figure 6D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claims.claim: Disruption of actin filaments, blocking of mRNA synthesis or protein production completely abrogated tumor cells' capacity to form a cell-in-cell formation.
claims.source: In sharp contrast, disruption of actin filaments, blocking of mRNA synthesis or protein production completely abrogated tumor cells' capacity to form a cell-in-cell formation, suggesting that the structure requires de novo synthesis of genes (Figure 6D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E using various inhibitors.

claims.claim: KEGG analysis indicated that multiple signaling cascades, including the JAK/STAT3 axis and FGF-receptors downstream pathways, are enriched in cell-in-cell formation generated in vivo.
claims.source: KEGG analysis further indicated that multiple signaling cascades, including the JAK/STAT3 axis and FGF-receptors downstream pathways, are enriched in cell-in-cell formation generated in vivo, with approximately 80 significantly elevated genes relating to these pathways (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, ).
claims.evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: EGR1 and STAT3 expression was significantly elevated in cell-in-cell tumors.
claims.source: Indeed, EGR1 and STAT3 expression was significantly elevated in cell-in-cell tumors (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Both mice and human tumors incubated with reactive T cells had elevated their p-STAT3 levels, in comparison to untreated tumor cells.
claims.source: Both mice and human tumors incubated with reactive T cells had elevated their p-STAT3 levels, in comparison to untreated tumor cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting this mechanism is conserved across species.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Overexpression of either STAT3 or EGR1 was sufficient to induce cell-in-cell formation without additional stimulation.
claims.source: Overexpression of either STAT3 or EGR1 was sufficient to induce cell-in-cell formation without additional stimulation (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: Cells overexpressing STAT3 or EGR1 were significantly more resistant to killing by CD8+ T cell, compared to sham transfected cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, these cells were significantly more resistant to killing by CD8+ T cell, compared to sham transfected cells (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 6I.

claims.claim: Inhibition of STAT3 and EGR1, but not MAPK3 and EGR2, significantly abrogated the capacity of tumor cells to form cell-in-cell structures upon incubation with IFNγ-stimulated T cells and with T cell secreted granules.
claims.source: Inhibition of STAT3 and EGR1, but not MAPK3 and EGR2, significantly abrogated the capacity of tumor cells to form cell-in-cell structures upon incubation with IFNγ-stimulated T cells and with T cell secreted granules (Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: Inhibition of STAT3, or EGR pathway, completely prevented cell-in-cell formation upon incubation with reactive T cells or T cell-secreted granules.
claims.source: We found that inhibition of STAT3, or EGR pathway, completely prevented cell-in-cell formation upon incubation with reactive T cells or T cell-secreted granules (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data using small molecule inhibitors shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Injection of Stattic prior to administration of immunotherapy partially restored the responsiveness of tumors that re-occur following immunotherapies.
claims.source: We found, however, that injection of Stattic prior to administration of immunotherapy partially restored the responsiveness of tumors that re-occur following immunotherapies (Figure 6K–L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6K-L.

claims.claim: Relapsed melanoma following treatment with pembrolizumab shares the majority of neoantigen with their corresponding primary tumors.
claims.source: Zaretsky JM. et al. found that relapsed melanoma following treatment with pembrolizumab shares the majority of neoantigen with their corresponding primary tumors (Zaretsky et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Non-small cells carcinoma (NSCC) relapsed following treatment with anti-PD1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint blockade bear similar neoantigen load, with only a relatively small number of putative deleted clones.
claims.source: Consistently, Anagnostou V. et al. found that non-small cells carcinoma (NSCC) relapsed following treatment with anti-PD1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint blockade bear similar neoantigen load, with only a relatively small number of putative deleted clones (Anagnostou et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Three out of four basal cell carcinomas patients treated with pembrolizumab exhibited similar neoantigen burden.
claims.source: In a recent study, Yost et al. demonstrated replenishment of T cell clones in basal cell carcinomas patients treated with pembrolizumab. Interestingly, three out of four analysed patients exhibited similar neoantigen burden (Yost et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claims.claim: Cell-in-cell structures generate multiple membrane layers, thus reducing the probability of compounds' internalization leading to increased tumor-cell survival.
claims.source: Here, we found that tumor cells escape T-cell-based immunotherapies by forming a transient cell-in-cell structure, and not by immunoediting. These structures generate multiple membrane layers, thus reducing the probability of compounds' internalization leading to increased tumor-cell survival.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The present cell-in-cell structure is triggered predominantly by reactive T cells, rather than glucose and nutrient starvation, mitosis, or loss of adherence.
claims.source: Although the present cell-in-cell structural falls within the definition entosis, it differs in several key elements: First, it is triggered predominantly by reactive T cells, rather than glucose and nutrient starvation (Hamann et al., 2017), mitosis (Durgan et al., 2017), or loss of adherence (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to published literature on entosis.

claims.claim: The cell-in-cell structure requires de novo synthesis of genes regulated by STAT3, and not through β-catenin signaling.
claims.source: Additionally, it requires de novo synthesis of genes regulated by STAT3, and not through β-catenin signaling (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data using inhibitors and gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: The cell-in-cell structure described is reversible and only rarely leads to cell cannibalism and apoptosis.
claims.source: Most importantly, the structure described here is reversible and only rarely leads to cell cannibalism and apoptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging showing dissemination of cells from the structure.

claims.claim: Only tumor cells that are capable to undergo 'spontaneous' entosis due to loss of cell adhesion can form cell-in-cell structure following interactions with reactive T cells.
claims.source: We found that only tumor cells that are capable to undergo 'spontaneous' entosis due to loss of cell adhesion, can form cell-in-cell structure following interactions with reactive T cells.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that hematopoietic cells do not form these structures.

claims.claim: Hematopoietic cells do not undergo 'spontaneous' or T-cell-mediated entosis but rather emperipolesis.
claims.source: In general, hematopoietic cells do no undergo entosis but rather emperipolesis (Krishna and Overholtzer, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Even in a model system where all the 'breaks' on T cell activity are removed, tumor cells may activate a STAT3 transcriptional program, which promotes spatial architecture impenetrable to cytotoxic mediators.
claims.source: This work also highlights a theoretical limitation of anti-tumor immunity, as even in a model system where all the 'breaks' on T cell activity are removed, tumor cells may activate a STAT3 transcriptional program, which promotes spatial architecture impenetrable to cytotoxic mediators.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Immune-mediated entosis should be inhibited prior to immunotherapy in order to reduce tumor resistance to subsequent drugs.
claims.source: Here, we suggest that immune-mediated entosis should be inhibited prior to immunotherapy in order to reduce tumor resistance to subsequent drugs.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings with Stattic treatment.

results.result: Multiple immunotherapy approaches in mouse models induce initial tumor regression followed by relapse with resistant tumors. Treatment with TNFα/CD40L/anti-TRP1 or adoptive transfer of gp100- or TRP2-reactive T cells led to tumor regression in all mice, but approximately half developed recurrent tumors resistant to subsequent treatments within 10 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1A-B showing tumor growth curves with initial regression followed by relapse. The data demonstrate reproducibility across different immunotherapy modalities and include appropriate controls and sample sizes.

results.result: Relapsed tumors maintain high levels of T cell infiltration with functional tumor-reactive T cells. Flow cytometry shows massive immune infiltration with dominant TRP2 and gp100-reactive T cell clones, and adoptive transfer of tumor-infiltrating T cells prevented tumor growth in naive mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 1C-D) and functional adoptive transfer experiments (Figure 1E-F). The data demonstrate that relapsed tumors are not escaping through lack of T cell infiltration or T cell dysfunction.

results.result: Relapsed tumors maintain expression of MHC-I, tumor antigens (TRP2, gp100), and comparable neoantigen burden to parental tumors. Whole exome sequencing and RNAseq analyses show similar neoantigen landscapes and gene expression patterns between relapsed and untreated B16F10 cells, with this pattern also observed in human melanoma and NSCLC patients following checkpoint blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are well-supported by multiple orthogonal approaches including flow cytometry, immunostaining, WES, and RNAseq (Figure 1G-M). The human relevance is supported by analysis of published patient data, though this relies on external datasets.

results.result: Resistance to immunotherapy is mediated by transient in vivo mechanisms rather than inherited genetic changes. Cell lines established from relapsed tumors regain susceptibility to immunotherapy when re-injected into mice and show similar killing susceptibility to parental cells in vitro, with RNAseq showing that established cell lines cluster together while freshly sorted cells from treated mice have distinct expression profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 are supported by in vivo tumor growth experiments (Figure 2A, C) and in vitro killing assays (Figure 2B, E), with PCA analysis (Figure 2F) supporting the transient nature of resistance. The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis that resistance is not genetically inherited.

results.result: Tumor cells surviving immunotherapy organize into transient cell-in-cell structures where multiple nuclei are surrounded by multiple membrane layers. Approximately half of surviving cells show this organization, with evidence from confocal microscopy, TEM, and histological sections. Dual-labeled tumor cells show mixing of GFP and tdTomato nuclei, and time-lapse imaging demonstrates spontaneous formation and dissemination of these structures in culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 are strongly supported by multiple imaging modalities including confocal microscopy (Figure 2G), TEM (Figure 2H), histology (Figure 2I), and quantitative analysis (Figure 2J). The dual-labeling experiments (Figure 2K) and time-lapse videos provide strong evidence against incomplete cell division as an explanation.

results.result: T cells, particularly CD8+ T cells, specifically induce cell-in-cell formation in tumor cells but not in normal epithelial cells. This phenomenon is T cell-dependent (absent in NSG mice), occurs across multiple mouse tumor types (with variation by tumor type), and is observed in human breast, colon, and melanoma tumors but not in lymphomas or glioblastomas.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by systematic testing across immune cell types (Figure 3A-B), NSG mouse experiments (Figure 3C), and screening of multiple tumor types in both mouse (Figure 3D) and human systems (Figure 3E). The specificity for T cells and tumor cells is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Cell-in-cell formations occur in human melanoma patients and are enriched in sites of T cell activity. Patient-derived melanoma cells form these structures when cultured with autologous TIL, xenografts treated with TIL show high prevalence of cell-in-cell structures, and in stage IV melanoma patients, these formations are abundant in T cell zones of draining lymph nodes but not primary tumors, with enrichment in recurrent versus primary tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by patient-derived cell experiments (Figure 3F-H), xenograft studies (Figure 3I), and histological analysis of patient samples (Figure 3J-M). The clinical relevance is well-established, though sample sizes are limited (n=4-6 patients).

results.result: T cell membrane-associated proteins, particularly those on secreted granules, mediate cell-in-cell formation. SEM shows intact granules on T cell membranes, isolated T cell granules are sufficient to induce cell-in-cell formation, and this is specific to T cells (not NK cells, macrophages, or other vesicles). Mass spectrometry identified ~400 proteins in T cell granules, and membrane-associated but not cytosolic or secreted proteins induce the formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 are supported by SEM analysis (Figure 4A), functional assays with isolated granules (Figure 4B-C), mass spectrometry (Figure 4D), and cell fractionation experiments (Figure 4G-H). The specificity is well-demonstrated through negative controls.

results.result: IFNγ-activated T cells are the primary mediators of cell-in-cell formation. T cells activated with IFNγ induce the most cell-in-cell formation compared to other activation methods, with distinct gene expression profiles. IFNγ-stimulated NK cells and macrophages can also induce formation at lower levels, and this mechanism is conserved in human T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C59-C62 are supported by systematic testing of different T cell activation conditions (Figure 4I), RNAseq analysis (Figure 4J), testing of other IFNγ-activated immune cells (Figure 4K), and human T cell experiments (Figure 4L). The data clearly establish IFNγ as the key activating signal.

results.result: Cell-in-cell structures protect tumor cells from T cell-mediated killing and chemotherapy by preventing penetration of cytotoxic molecules to inner cells. Single tumor cells are significantly more susceptible to killing than cell-in-cell tumors, with T cells forming normal immunological synapses and creating pores in outer cells, but granzyme B and perforin distribution is limited to outer cells, leaving inner cells intact. This protection extends to chemotherapies and free radicals.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C71 are comprehensively supported by caspase 3/7 assays (Figure 5A, J), in vivo tumor growth studies (Figure 5B), SEM analysis (Figure 5C-D), super-resolution microscopy of immunological synapses (Figure 5E-G), immunostaining for granzyme B and perforin (Figure 5H-I), and viability assays with various compounds (Figure 5K). The mechanism of protection is well-characterized.

results.result: Cell-in-cell formation is a ROCK-dependent entosis-like process requiring de novo gene synthesis but distinct from classical entosis. Cells maintain separate cytoplasms without fusion, ROCK inhibition prevents formation, but unlike classical entosis, it does not require β-catenin, E-cadherin, N-cadherin, or Wnt signaling. Disruption of actin filaments or blocking mRNA/protein synthesis prevents formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 are supported by dual-labeling experiments (Figure 6A, supplementary), ROCK inhibitor studies (Figure 6B-C), and systematic testing of various inhibitors (Figure 6D-E). The data clearly distinguish this process from classical entosis while establishing its mechanistic requirements.

results.result: STAT3 and EGR1 signaling pathways govern cell-in-cell formation. KEGG analysis shows enrichment of JAK/STAT3 and FGF-receptor pathways, with elevated EGR1 and STAT3 expression and phospho-STAT3 levels in cell-in-cell tumors (conserved in human cells). Overexpression of either STAT3 or EGR1 is sufficient to induce formation and confer resistance to T cell killing, while inhibition of STAT3 or EGR1 (but not MAPK3 or EGR2) prevents formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C79-C85 are well-supported by KEGG pathway analysis, gene expression data (Figure 6G), immunostaining (supplementary), overexpression experiments (Figure 6H-I), and siRNA/inhibitor studies (Figure 6J, supplementary). The specificity of STAT3/EGR1 versus other related factors strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Inhibiting STAT3 prior to immunotherapy improves therapeutic efficacy in relapsed tumors. Treatment with Stattic (STAT3 inhibitor) before immunotherapy partially restored responsiveness in tumors that recurred following initial immunotherapy in two different treatment models.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C86 are supported by in vivo tumor growth experiments (Figure 6K-L) showing that Stattic pretreatment improves response to both adoptive T cell transfer and antibody-based immunotherapy. However, the improvement is described as 'partial,' and the mechanism could involve effects beyond cell-in-cell inhibition.

results.result: Background context on immunotherapy resistance and neoantigen retention in relapsed tumors. The manuscript establishes that most patients experience partial response and relapse, that relapsed tumors share neoantigens with primary tumors (contrary to immunoediting predictions), and that current combination therapies remain insufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C17, C87-C89 provide literature context supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the rationale for the study but are not novel findings of this work. The citations appear appropriate and the general knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

results.result: Interpretive framework and implications of the cell-in-cell mechanism. The authors propose that tumor cells escape immunotherapy through transient cell-in-cell structures that generate multiple membrane layers preventing compound internalization, that this differs from classical entosis in key mechanistic features, and that this represents a fundamental limitation of immunotherapy that should be targeted prophylactically.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C90-C97 represent interpretations and implications of the experimental findings. While these are largely supported by the data presented, some claims (particularly C96-C97 about theoretical limitations and therapeutic recommendations) extend beyond what the data directly demonstrate. The distinction from classical entosis (C91-C93) is well-supported.
